title: Chapter 39
paragraphs: I was twenty-three years of age. Not another word had I heard to enlighten me on the subject of my expectations, and my twenty-third birthday was a week gone. We had left Barnard's Inn more than a year ago and lived in the Temple. Our rooms were in Garden Court, down by the river.

Mr. Pocket and I had for some time parted ways as to our original arrangement, though we continued on the best terms. Despite my inability to settle to anything — which I hope arose from the restless and uncertain hold on which I held my fortune — I had a taste for reading and read regularly so many hours a day. The matter of Herbert's was still progressing, and everything with me was as I have brought it down to the close of the last chapter.

Business had taken Herbert on a journey to Marseilles. I was alone and had a dull sense of being alone. Dispirited and anxious, long hoping that tomorrow or next week would clear my way, and long disappointed, I sadly missed the cheerful face and ready response of my friend.

It was wretched weather — stormy and wet, stormy and wet — and mud, mud, mud, deep in all the streets. Day after day, a vast heavy curtain had been driving over London from the East, and it drove still, as if in the East there were an eternity of cloud and wind. So furious had been the gusts that high buildings in town had had the lead stripped off their roofs. In the country, trees had been torn up and sails of windmills carried away. Gloomy reports had come in from the coast, of shipwreck and death. Violent blasts of rain had accompanied these rages of wind, and the day just ended as I sat down to read had been the worst of all.

Changes have been made in that part of the Temple since then, and it has not now so lonely a character as it had then, nor is it so exposed to the river. We lived at the top of the last house, and the wind rushing up the river shook the house that night like cannon fire, or the breaking of a sea. When the rain came with it and dashed against the windows, I thought, raising my eyes to them as they shook, that I might have fancied myself in a storm-beaten lighthouse. Occasionally the smoke came rolling down the chimney as though it could not bear to go out into such a night. When I set the doors open and looked down the staircase, the staircase lamps were blown out. When I shielded my face with my hands and looked through the black windows — opening them even slightly was out of the question in the teeth of such wind and rain — I saw that the lamps in the court were blown out, that the lamps on the bridges and the shore were shuddering, and that the coal fires in barges on the river were being carried away before the wind like red-hot splashes in the rain.

I read with my watch on the table, intending to close my book at eleven o'clock. As I shut it, Saint Paul's and all the many church clocks in the City — some leading, some accompanying, some following — struck that hour. The sound was curiously distorted by the wind. I was listening and thinking how the wind assailed and tore it when I heard a footstep on the stair.

What nervous foolishness made me start and terrifyingly connect it with the footstep of my dead sister matters not. It was past in a moment, and I listened again and heard the footstep stumble in coming on. Remembering then that the staircase lights were blown out, I took up my reading lamp and went out to the stair-head. Whoever was below had stopped on seeing my lamp, for all was quiet.
"There is someone down there, is there not?" I called out, looking down.
"Yes," said a voice from the darkness beneath.
"What floor do you want?"
"The top. Mr. Pip."
"That is my name. — There is nothing the matter?"
"Nothing the matter," returned the voice. And the man came on.

I stood with my lamp held out over the stair rail, and he came slowly within its light. It was a shaded lamp, made to shine upon a book, and its circle of light was very small. So he was in it for a mere instant and then out of it. In that instant I had seen a face that was strange to me, looking up with an incomprehensible air of being touched and pleased by the sight of me.

Moving the lamp as the man moved, I made out that he was solidly dressed, but roughly, like a traveler by sea. That he had long iron-grey hair. That his age was about sixty. That he was a muscular man, strong on his legs, and that he was browned and hardened by exposure to weather. As he climbed the last stair or two, and the light of my lamp included us both, I saw, with a stupid kind of amazement, that he was holding out both his hands to me.
"Pray what is your business?" I asked him.
"My business?" he repeated, pausing. "Ah! Yes. I will explain my business, by your leave."
"Do you wish to come in?"
"Yes," he replied. "I wish to come in, master."

I had asked him the question inhospitably enough, for I resented the sort of bright and gratified recognition that still shone in his face. I resented it because it seemed to imply that he expected me to respond to it. But I took him into the room I had just left, and having set the lamp on the table, asked him as civilly as I could to explain himself.

He looked about him with the strangest air — an air of wondering pleasure, as if he had some part in the things he admired — and he pulled off a rough outer coat and his hat. Then I saw that his head was furrowed and bald, and that the long iron-grey hair grew only on its sides. But I saw nothing that in the least explained him. On the contrary, I saw him next moment, once more holding out both his hands to me.
"What do you mean?" I said, half suspecting him to be mad.

He stopped looking at me and slowly rubbed his right hand over his head. "It's disappointing to a man," he said in a coarse broken voice, "after having looked forward so long and come so far. But you're not to blame for that — neither of us is to blame for that. I'll speak in half a minute. Give me half a minute, please."
He sat down on a chair that stood before the fire and covered his forehead with his large brown veined hands. I looked at him closely then and drew back a little from him. But I did not know him.
"There's no one near," he said, looking over his shoulder, "is there?"
"Why do you, a stranger coming into my rooms at this time of night, ask that question?" I said.

"You're a bold one," he returned, shaking his head at me with a deliberate affection at once most baffling and most exasperating. "I'm glad you've grown up a bold one! But don't grab hold of me. You'd be sorry afterward to have done it."

I abandoned the intention he had detected, for I knew him! Even yet I could not recall a single feature, but I knew him! If the wind and the rain had driven away the intervening years, had scattered all the intervening objects, had swept us to the churchyard where we first stood face to face on such different levels, I could not have known my convict more distinctly than I knew him now as he sat in the chair before the fire. No need to take a file from his pocket and show it to me. No need to take the handkerchief from his neck and twist it round his head. No need to hug himself with both his arms and take a shivering turn across the room, looking back at me for recognition. I knew him before he gave me any of those clues, though a moment before I had not been conscious of remotely suspecting his identity.

He came back to where I stood and again held out both his hands. Not knowing what to do — for in my astonishment I had lost my composure — I reluctantly gave him my hands. He grasped them heartily, raised them to his lips, kissed them, and still held them.
"You acted noble, my boy," he said. "Noble, Pip! And I have never forgot it!"
At a change in his manner, as if he were even going to embrace me, I laid a hand upon his breast and pushed him away.

"Stay!" I said. "Keep off! If you are grateful to me for what I did when I was a little child, I hope you have shown your gratitude by mending your way of life. If you have come here to thank me, it was not necessary. Still, however you have found me out, there must be something good in the feeling that has brought you here, and I will not repulse you. But surely you must understand that — I —"
My attention was so arrested by the singularity of his fixed look at me that the words died away on my tongue.
"You was saying," he observed, when we had confronted one another in silence, "that surely I must understand. What, surely must I understand?"

"That I cannot wish to renew that chance encounter with you of long ago, under these different circumstances. I am glad to believe you have repented and recovered yourself. I am glad to tell you so. I am glad that, thinking I deserve to be thanked, you have come to thank me. But our ways are different ways, nonetheless. You are wet, and you look weary. Will you drink something before you go?"

He had loosely replaced his neckerchief and had stood keenly observing me, biting a long end of it. "I think," he answered, still with the end at his mouth and still watching me, "that I will drink — I thank you — before I go."

There was a tray ready on a side table. I brought it to the table near the fire and asked him what he would have. He touched one of the bottles without looking at it or speaking, and I made him some hot rum and water. I tried to keep my hand steady while I did so, but his look at me as he leaned back in his chair with the long draggled end of his neckerchief between his teeth — evidently forgotten — made my hand very difficult to master. When at last I put the glass to him, I saw with amazement that his eyes were full of tears.

Up to this time I had remained standing, so as not to disguise that I wished him gone. But I was softened by the softened look of the man and felt a touch of reproach. "I hope," I said, hurriedly pouring something into a glass for myself and drawing a chair to the table, "that you will not think I spoke harshly to you just now. I had no intention of doing it, and I am sorry for it if I did. I wish you well and happy!"

As I put my glass to my lips, he glanced with surprise at the end of his neckerchief, dropping from his mouth as he opened it, and stretched out his hand. I gave him mine, and then he drank and drew his sleeve across his eyes and forehead.
"How are you living?" I asked him.
"I've been a sheep farmer, stock breeder, other trades besides, away in the new world," he said. "Many a thousand miles of stormy water off from this."
"I hope you have done well?"
"I've done wonderfully well. There's others went out along with me that have done well too, but no man has done nearly as well as me. I'm famous for it."
"I am glad to hear it."
"I hope to hear you say so, my dear boy."
Without stopping to try to understand those words or the tone in which they were spoken, I turned to a point that had just come into my mind.
"Have you ever seen a messenger you once sent to me," I asked, "since he undertook that errand?"
"Never set eyes on him. I wasn't likely to."

"He came faithfully, and he brought me the two one-pound notes. I was a poor boy then, as you know, and to a poor boy they were a little fortune. But like you, I have done well since, and you must let me pay them back. You can put them to some other poor boy's use." I took out my purse.

He watched me as I laid my purse on the table and opened it, and he watched me as I separated two one-pound notes from its contents. They were clean and new, and I spread them out and handed them over to him. Still watching me, he laid them one upon the other, folded them lengthwise, gave them a twist, set fire to them at the lamp, and dropped the ashes into the tray.

"May I make so bold," he said then, with a smile that was like a frown and with a frown that was like a smile, "as to ask you how you have done well, since you and me was out on them lone shivering marshes?"
"How?"
"Ah!"

He emptied his glass, got up, and stood at the side of the fire, with his heavy brown hand on the mantelshelf. He put a foot up to the bars to dry, and the wet boot began to steam. But he neither looked at it, nor at the fire, but steadily looked at me. It was only now that I began to tremble.
When my lips had parted and had shaped some words that were without sound, I forced myself to tell him — though I could not do it clearly — that I had been chosen to succeed to some property.
"Might a mere vermin ask what property?" he said.
I faltered, "I don't know."
"Might a mere vermin ask whose property?" he said.
I faltered again, "I don't know."
"Could I make a guess, I wonder," said the convict, "at your income since you came of age? As to the first figure, now. Five?"
With my heart beating like a heavy hammer of disordered action, I rose out of my chair and stood with my hand on the back of it, looking wildly at him.

"Concerning a guardian," he went on. "There ought to have been some guardian, or such-like, while you was a minor. Some lawyer, maybe. As to the first letter of that lawyer's name, now. Would it be J?"

The whole truth of my position flashed upon me. Its disappointments, its dangers, its disgraces, every kind of consequence rushed in at once. I went down under the weight of them and had to struggle for every breath.

"Put it," he resumed, "as the employer of that lawyer whose name began with a J, and might be Jaggers — put it as he had come over sea to Portsmouth and had landed there, and had wanted to come on to you. 'However, you have found me out,' you says just now. Well! However did I find you out? Why, I wrote from Portsmouth to a person in London, for particulars of your address. That person's name? Why, Wemmick."

I couldn’t have spoken a word to save my life. I stood with one hand on the back of the chair and one on my chest, where I seemed to be suffocating. There I stood, staring wildly at him, until the room began to heave and spin and I clutched at the chair. He caught me, drew me to the sofa and propped me against the cushions. Down he went on one knee before me, bringing that face I now remembered so well, the face I shuddered at, very close to mine.

"Yes, Pip, dear boy, I've made a gentleman of you! It's me what has done it! I swore that time, sure as ever I earned a guinea, that guinea should go to you. I swore afterward, sure as ever I speculated and got rich you should get rich. I lived rough so that you should live smooth. I worked hard so that you could be above work. What odds, dear boy? Do I tell it, for you to feel an obligation? Not a bit. I tell it, for you to know as that there hunted dunghill dog what you kept life in got his head so high that he could make a gentleman — and, Pip, you're him!"
The horror in which I held the man, the dread I had of him, the revulsion with which I shrank from him, could not have been exceeded if he had been some terrible beast.

“Look here, Pip. I’m your second father. You’re my son — more to me than any son. I’ve put money by just for you to spend. When I was a hired shepherd in a lonely hut, never seeing any faces but sheep’s faces till I half forgot what men and women looked like, I saw yours. Many a time I dropped my knife in that hut, eating my dinner or my supper, and I says, ‘Here’s the boy again, looking at me while I eat and drink!’ Many’s the time I saw you there, plain as I ever saw you on them misty marshes. ‘Lord strike me dead!’ I says each time — and I’d go outside to say it under the open sky — ‘if I get my freedom and my money and don’t make that boy a gentleman!’ And I done it. Why, look at you, dear boy! Look at these lodgings of yours, fit for a lord! A lord? Ah! You shall match money with lords for a wager, and beat ’em!”
In the heat of his triumph, and knowing I had nearly fainted, he didn’t notice how I took all this. That was my one grain of relief.

"Look here!" he went on, taking my watch out of my pocket and turning toward him a ring on my finger while I recoiled from his touch as if he had been a snake. "A gold one and a beauty — that's a gentleman's, I hope! A diamond all set round with rubies — that's a gentleman's, I hope! Look at your linen — fine and beautiful! Look at your clothes — better ain't to be got! And your books too," turning his eyes round the room, "mounting up, on their shelves, by hundreds! And you read them, don't you? I see you've been a reading of them when I come in. Ha, ha, ha! You shall read them to me, dear boy! And if they're in foreign languages that I don't understand, I shall be just as proud as if I did."
Again he took both my hands and put them to his lips, while my blood ran cold within me.

“Don’t you trouble to speak, Pip,” he said, drawing his sleeve across his eyes and forehead again, with that click in his throat I remembered so well. He was all the more horrible to me for being so much in earnest. “Best thing you can do is keep quiet, dear boy. You haven’t looked forward to this the long way round as I have. You weren’t ready for it like I was. But didn’t you ever think it might be me?”
"Oh no, no, no," I returned. "Never, never!"
"Well, you see it was me, and single-handed. Never a soul in it but my own self and Mr. Jaggers."
"Was there no one else?" I asked.

"No," he said, with a glance of surprise. "Who else should there be? And, dear boy, how good-looking you have grown! There's bright eyes somewhere — eh? Isn't there bright eyes somewhere, what you love the thoughts of?"
Oh Estella, Estella!

"They shall be yours, dear boy, if money can buy them. Not that a gentleman like you, so well set up as you, can't win them off his own game. But money shall back you! Let me finish what I was going to tell you, dear boy. From that there hut and that there hiring-out, I got money left me by my master (which died, and had been the same as me), and I got my liberty and went for myself. In every single thing I went for, I went for you. 'Lord strike a blight upon it,' I says, whatever it was I went for, 'if it ain't for him!' It all prospered wonderful. As I gave you to understand just now, I'm famous for it. It was the money left me, and the gains of the first few year, what I sent home to Mr. Jaggers — all for you — when he first come after you, agreeable to my letter."
Oh, that he had never come! That he had left me at the forge — far from contented, yet, by comparison, happy!

"And then, dear boy, it was a reward for me, look here, to know in secret that I was making a gentleman. The blood horses of them colonists might fling up the dust over me as I was walking. What do I say? I says to myself, 'I'm making a better gentleman than ever you'll be!' When one of them says to another, 'He was a convict, a few year ago, and is an ignorant common fellow now, for all he's lucky,' what do I say? I says to myself, 'If I ain't a gentleman, nor yet ain't got no learning, I'm the owner of such. All on you owns stock and land. Which on you owns a brought-up London gentleman?' This way I kept myself agoing. And this way I kept my mind fixed on coming back one day and see my boy, and make myself known to him, on his own ground."
He laid his hand on my shoulder. I shuddered at the thought that for anything I knew, his hand might be stained with blood.

"It warn't easy, Pip, for me to leave those parts, nor yet it warn't safe. But I held to it, and the harder it was, the stronger I held, for I was determined, and my mind firm made up. At last I done it. Dear boy, I done it!"

I tried to collect my thoughts, but I was stunned. All along I seemed to have been listening more to the wind and rain than to him. Even now I couldn’t separate his voice from theirs, though theirs were loud and his was silent.
"Where will you put me?" he asked presently. "I must be put somewhere, dear boy."
"To sleep?" I said.
"Yes. And to sleep long and sound," he answered. "For I've been sea-tossed and sea-washed, months and months."
"My friend and companion," I said, rising from the sofa, "is absent. You must have his room."
"He won't come back tomorrow, will he?"
"No," I said, answering almost mechanically despite my utmost efforts. "Not tomorrow."
"Because, look here, dear boy," he said, dropping his voice and laying a long finger on my breast in an impressive manner, "caution is necessary."
"How do you mean? Caution?"
"By God, it's death!"
"What's death?"
"I was sent for life. It's death to come back. There's been too much coming back of late years, and I should certainly be hanged if they caught me."

This was all that was needed! The wretched man, after loading wretched me with his gold and silver chains for years, had risked his life to come to me, and here it lay in my keeping! If I had loved him instead of loathing him, if the strongest admiration and affection had drawn me to him instead of the strongest disgust making me shrink away, it could have been no worse. It would in fact have been better, for then the wish to keep him safe would have come naturally and tenderly to my heart.

My first thought was to close the shutters so no light could be seen from outside, then to close and fasten the doors. As I did so he stood at the table drinking rum and eating biscuit. To see him there was to see my convict at his meal on the marshes again. I half expected him to bend down at any moment and start filing at his leg.

I went into Herbert’s room and closed off every way from it to the staircase except through the room where we had been talking. Then I asked him if he would go to bed. Yes, he said, but could he have some of my “gentleman’s linen” to put on in the morning? I brought it out and laid it ready for him, and again my blood ran cold when he took both my hands in his to say goodnight.

I got away from him, I don’t know how, stirred up the fire in the room where we had sat together and sat down beside it, afraid to go to bed. For an hour or more I was too stunned to think. Only when I began to think did I begin to take in what a wreck I was, and how the ship I’d sailed in had gone to pieces.

Miss Havisham’s designs for me, all a mere dream. Estella never meant for me. I had only been tolerated at Satis House as a convenience, a sting for the greedy relations, a dummy with a mechanical heart to practise on when there was nobody else handy. Those were the first stabs of pain. But the sharpest and deepest of all was this: it was for a convict, guilty of I knew not what crimes, liable to be dragged from the very rooms where I sat thinking and hanged at the Old Bailey door, that I had deserted Joe.

I would not have gone back to Joe now. I would not have gone back to Biddy now, for any consideration. Simply, I suppose, because my sense of my own worthless conduct toward them was greater than every consideration. No wisdom on earth could have given me the comfort that I should have derived from their simplicity and fidelity. But I could never, never undo what I had done.

In every furious gust of wind, in every rush of rain, I heard pursuers. Twice I could have sworn there was a knock and a whisper at the outer door. In my fear I began to imagine, or to remember, that I’d had mysterious warnings of his approach. That for weeks I’d passed faces in the street I thought like his. That as he came nearer across the sea, those likenesses had multiplied. That somehow his wicked spirit had sent these messengers to mine, and that now, on this stormy night, he’d kept his word and was with me.

Another thought crowded in upon these. With my own childish eyes I had seen him to be a desperately violent man. I had heard the other convict say over and over that he had tried to murder him. I had seen him down in the ditch tearing and fighting like a wild beast. From these memories I drew into the firelight a half-formed fear that it might be unsafe to be shut in there with him in the dead of that wild and lonely night. The fear swelled until it filled the room and drove me to take a candle and go and look at my dreadful burden.

He had tied a handkerchief round his head. His sleeping face was set and grim. But he was asleep, and quietly too, though a pistol lay on his pillow. Once I was sure, I quietly slipped the key into the outside of his door and locked him in before I sat down by the fire again. Little by little I slid off the chair and lay on the floor. Even in sleep I had never lost the sense of my misery. When I woke, the church clocks to the east were striking five, the candles had guttered out, the fire was dead, and the wind and rain deepened the thick black darkness.
THIS IS THE END OF THE SECOND STAGE OF PIP'S EXPECTATIONS.
